review.reason: Excavation tests a historical tradition; distinguishes physical evidence from interpretation.

item.title: A major monastic centre? Rethinking Lismore’s place in the ecclesiastical landscapes of early medieval Britain
item.headline: Broken casting moulds reveal Lismore’s skilled medieval community
item.authors: Clare Ellis, Angela Boyle, Gemma Cruickshanks, Nicholas Evans, Robert Hay, Edouard Masson-MacLean, Joshua Wright and Gordon Noble
item.summary: Graves and workshop debris strengthen the case for an important early medieval monastery on Scotland’s Lismore. Its earliest church remains unidentified.

evidence.question: What survives of Lismore’s early religious community?
evidence.method: Community-led excavations combined geophysical surveys, radiocarbon dating, artefact comparison and X-ray fluorescence metal analysis.
evidence.limitations: Only parts of the site are excavated; enclosure boundaries remain uncertain.

explainer.finding: Seventh–ninth-century workshop layers contained moulds and crucibles, including evidence of copper-alloy, silver and gold casting.
explainer.method: Researchers linked dated deposits to manufacturing debris; metal residues helped identify what craftspeople cast.
explainer.meaning: A brooch could arrive through trade. A broken brooch mould instead points to local production, revealing skills that chronicles may overlook.
explainer.limits: Craftworkers were not necessarily monks. These finds do not directly establish the traditional sixth-century foundation.
